name: Algeria

pinned on a flag badge: blue, gold, blue with a black three-pointed trident in the middle
picked up a bundle of bills called the Barbadian dollar at the bank

greeting.text: People here speak English, so just say hello with a warm "Hello!"

name: Belize
arrival: Belize sits on the Caribbean coast of Central America. It is known for a giant round ocean sinkhole called the Great Blue Hole, a huge barrier reef, ancient Maya cities in the jungle, and the world's first jaguar reserve.

hints.text: studied a map of a small country tucked on the Caribbean coast of Central America
wanted to dive into a giant, near-perfect round sinkhole in the middle of the sea
traced a flag: deep blue with a red stripe top and bottom and two woodcutters in a white circle
tucked away a purse of leftover Belize dollars for the trip

greeting.text: People here speak English, so just say hello with a friendly "Hello!"

name: Colombia
arrival: Colombia is a large country in northern South America touching both the Pacific and the Caribbean. It has snowy Andes peaks, thick Amazon rainforest, more kinds of birds than any other country, and a river that turns bright red.

hints.text: mapped out a big country at the very top of South America, touching two oceans
sewed a flag patch on a backpack — a wide yellow band on top with blue and red below it
pointed at a guidebook page picturing Colombian peso notes

greeting.text: In Spanish, hello is "Hola" (OH-lah).

name: Costa Rica
arrival: This small, green country in Central America is famous for lush rainforests, misty cloud forests, and rumbling volcanoes. Bursting with wildlife, it gave up its whole army long ago to spend more on schools.

hints.text: packed for a small, green land of rainforests and rumbling volcanoes in Central America
loved that this peaceful place got rid of its entire army long ago
eyed a flag in a guidebook: blue and white stripes with a wide red band across the middle
swapped travelers' cheques for a roll of bills called colones

greeting.text: Most people speak Spanish — say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Cuba
arrival: This is the largest island in the whole Caribbean, known for lovingly kept 1950s cars rolling through Havana, hand-rolled cigars, and lively salsa and son music drifting from its sunny streets.

hints.text: chattered about the biggest island in the whole Caribbean Sea
was thrilled to cruise past old buildings in a shiny 1950s American car
kept humming salsa tunes and bragging about famous hand-rolled cigars
drew a flag with blue and white stripes and a single white star in a red triangle
showed off a lucky coin called the Cuban peso

greeting.text: Most people speak Spanish — say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Dominica
arrival: This tiny, mountainous island in the eastern Caribbean is nicknamed the “Nature Island” for its wild rainforests, hundreds of rushing rivers, a steaming boiling lake, and whales that swim offshore all year.

hints.text: asked about ferries to a tiny, wild island in the eastern Caribbean
was itching to peer into a steaming lake that bubbles and boils like a huge pot
nicknamed it the “Nature Island” and raved about a rainforest with rivers everywhere
doodled a green flag with a cross of yellow, black, and white and a purple-and-green parrot in a red circle at the center

greeting.text: The official language is English, but many people also greet you in Kwéyòl (a French Creole) with “Bonjou” (bon-ZHOO).

name: Dominican Republic
arrival: This warm Caribbean country shares one island with Haiti. Its capital, Santo Domingo, is the oldest European-built city in the Americas, and the whole nation loves bouncy merengue music and baseball.

hints.text: booked a ticket toward a sunny country that shares its island with a neighbor in the Caribbean
wanted to explore the oldest European-built city anywhere in the Americas
practiced dance steps for bouncy merengue and bachata music
sketched a flag split into blue and red boxes with a white cross running through it

greeting.text: Most people speak Spanish — say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Ecuador
arrival: This South American country sits right on the equator — the “middle of the world.” It's known for snow-capped volcanoes, thick Amazon rainforest, and the far-off Galápagos Islands full of unique animals.

hints.text: studied a map of South America looking for the country the equator runs straight through
couldn't wait to stand on the very line marking the “middle of the world”
dreamed of meeting giant tortoises and blue-footed birds on faraway islands
doodled a flag with yellow, blue, and red stripes and a condor perched over a mountain

greeting.text: Most people speak Spanish — say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: El Salvador
arrival: El Salvador is the smallest and most crowded country in Central America, nicknamed the "Land of Volcanoes." It is the only nation here with no Caribbean coast, so its beaches all face the Pacific Ocean.

hints.text: circled the smallest, most crowded country in Central America on a map
kept talking about a "Land of Volcanoes" dotted with steaming, cone-shaped mountains
traced a flag — a blue stripe, a white stripe, and another blue stripe with a little emblem in the middle

greeting.text: Most people speak Spanish — say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Grenada
arrival: Grenada is a tiny Caribbean island known as the "Spice Isle" because it grows so much nutmeg. It has famous beaches like Grand Anse and an underwater sculpture park where statues stand on the seabed.

hints.text: kept talking about heading to a tiny spice-growing island in the Caribbean
kept sniffing jars of nutmeg and cinnamon from a place called the "Spice Isle"
wanted to dive down to an underwater park where statues stand on the seabed
stuck a flag sticker on a suitcase — a red border with green and yellow triangles, seven little stars, and a tiny nutmeg

greeting.text: People speak English here — just say “Hello!” with a warm island smile.

name: Guatemala
arrival: Guatemala is a Central American country packed with volcanoes and ancient Maya temples. The stone pyramids of Tikal rise above the rainforest, and beautiful Lake Atitlan sits ringed by three towering volcanoes.

hints.text: planned a trip to a Central American country full of steaming volcanoes
wanted to climb ancient stone pyramids poking up above the rainforest at Tikal
pinned on a flag badge — a blue stripe, a white stripe, and a blue stripe, with a bright green bird in the middle
admired a banknote called the quetzal, named after a bright green rainforest bird

greeting.text: Most people speak Spanish — say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Guyana
region: the north coast of South America
arrival: This country on the northern coast of South America is almost entirely covered in rainforest, home to the thundering Kaieteur Falls — and, unusually for the continent, English-speaking and cricket-mad.

hints.text: raved about one of the tallest single-drop waterfalls in the world, deep in the rainforest
couldn't stop talking about a South American country that's cricket-mad and feels a bit Caribbean
sketched a flag — green with a big golden arrow and a red triangle, the “Golden Arrowhead”
admired a banknote showing a bird and a waterfall, called the Guyanese dollar

greeting.text: A surprise — it's the only country in South America where English is the official language, so just say “Hello.”

name: Haiti
arrival: Haiti shares the mountainous island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic, and its name means "land of high mountains." It is famous for brightly painted "tap-tap" buses, colorful folk art, and a giant mountaintop fortress.

hints.text: kept repeating that the country's name means "land of high mountains"
couldn't wait to ride the brightly painted "tap-tap" buses covered in colorful pictures
sewed a flag patch on a backpack — a blue band above a red band with a little palm tree in the center
asked the bank for a bundle of banknotes called the gourde

greeting.text: People speak Haitian Creole — say hello with “Bonjou” (bohn-ZHOO).

name: Honduras
arrival: Honduras is a mountainous Central American country that was once a famous "banana republic." It has ancient Maya ruins at Copan, and the island of Roatan sits on a huge coral reef in the Caribbean Sea.

hints.text: kept talking about giant banana plantations in an old "banana republic"
planned to explore the Maya ruins of Copan, with a stone stairway carved full of picture-writing
studied a flag in a guidebook — a blue stripe, a white stripe, and a blue stripe with five little blue stars in the middle
packed a purse of leftover lempira, named after a brave Indigenous chief

greeting.text: Most people speak Spanish — say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Jamaica
arrival: This mountainous island in the Caribbean is the birthplace of reggae music and its most famous singer, home to record-breaking sprinters, and known for fiery jerk cooking and the terraced waterfalls of Dunn's River.

hints.text: kept humming bouncy reggae tunes and talking about the island's most famous singer
couldn't wait to climb a giant staircase of waterfalls that tumble down toward the beach
traced a flag with a golden X splitting it into green and black triangles
counted out crisp banknotes called the Jamaican dollar

greeting.text: The official language is English, but locals greet you in Patois with “Wah gwaan” (wah-GWAHN), meaning “what's going on?”

name: Nicaragua
arrival: This is the largest country in Central America, known for its chain of smoking volcanoes, a huge freshwater lake with a volcano-island in the middle, and colorful old colonial towns.

hints.text: talked about an island made of two volcanoes sitting in a giant lake
sketched a flag — blue, white, blue with a ring of volcanoes in the middle
traded a stack of cash for colorful bills called the córdoba

greeting.text: Like much of Latin America, people here speak Spanish — say “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Panama
arrival: This narrow country in Central America links North and South America, and its world-famous canal lets giant ships sail between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans through the thin strip of land.

hints.text: studied a map of a skinny, curving country in Central America
kept talking about a huge canal where enormous ships pass between two oceans
couldn't wait to visit tiny palm-covered islands where the Guna people live
stuck a flag sticker on a suitcase — four squares: a red one, a blue one, and two white ones each holding a star
showed off a shiny coin called the balboa

greeting.text: People speak Spanish here — say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Paraguay
arrival: This landlocked country in the heart of South America is known for the Guaraní language spoken by nearly everyone, the enormous Itaipú Dam on its rivers, and the wild scrublands of the Gran Chaco.

hints.text: asked about buses to a landlocked country in the middle of South America
practiced speaking Guaraní, an Indigenous language most people there share alongside Spanish
pinned on a flag badge with red, white, and blue stripes and a little round star emblem in the middle
asked the bank for a bundle of banknotes called the guaraní

greeting.text: In Guaraní, hello is “Mba'éichapa” (mba-EY-cha-pah).

name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
arrival: This two-island country in the Caribbean is made of green volcanic hills, home to a huge stone fortress high on a hilltop and a sleeping volcano, Mount Liamuiga, wrapped in rainforest.

hints.text: wanted to explore a giant stone fortress perched high on a hill above the sea
planned to hike up a sleeping volcano with a rainforest crater at its top
sewed a flag patch on a backpack — a black diagonal band, two white stars, and green and red triangles

greeting.text: People here speak English — a warm island “Hello!” works everywhere.

name: Saint Lucia
arrival: This lush island in the eastern Caribbean is famous for the twin Pitons — two pointed volcanic peaks rising straight out of the sea — plus steamy sulphur springs and warm, mineral-rich mud baths.

hints.text: couldn't wait to see two pointy volcanic peaks poking straight up out of the ocean
wanted to drive right up to a bubbling volcano and soak in warm, muddy springs
kept saying this was the only country named after a woman
studied a flag in a guidebook: a blue banner with a black-and-yellow triangle shaped like a mountain peak

greeting.text: Many Saint Lucians speak Kwéyòl, a French creole — say hello with “Bonjou” (bon-ZHOO).

name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
arrival: This nation of one main island plus a string of tiny Grenadine islands sits in the eastern Caribbean. It is known for the rumbling La Soufrière volcano, black-sand beaches, and the coral-ringed Tobago Cays.

hints.text: packed a snorkel to swim in a ring of tiny sandy cays surrounded by coral reefs
drew a flag with blue, yellow, and green stripes and three little green diamonds shaped like a V
kept saying palm-lined coves there had starred as a hideout in pirate movies

greeting.text: People here speak English — just say hello with a big “Hello!” (heh-LOH).

name: Suriname
arrival: This is the smallest country in South America, tucked on the northern Atlantic coast. Almost all of it is thick rainforest, and its capital, Paramaribo, is famous for old wooden Dutch buildings.

hints.text: packed a bag for the smallest country on the whole continent of South America
hoped to watch giant leatherback turtles crawl ashore to lay eggs on quiet beaches
sketched a flag with green, white, and red stripes and a single yellow star in the middle
swapped travelers' cheques for a roll of banknotes called the Surinamese dollar

greeting.text: The official language is Dutch, where hello is “Hallo” (HAH-loh), but many people also say “Fa waka” in Sranan Tongo.

name: Trinidad and Tobago
arrival: These twin islands are the southernmost in the Caribbean, sitting just off the coast of Venezuela. They are the birthplace of steelpan drums and famous for a giant, colorful Carnival and flocks of scarlet ibis.

hints.text: circled two little islands right at the bottom of the Caribbean, close to South America
couldn't wait to dance at a huge, colorful Carnival full of feathers and costumes
stuck a flag sticker on a suitcase — red, with a black diagonal stripe edged in white
counted out crisp banknotes called the Trinidad and Tobago dollar

greeting.text: People here speak English — greet a friend with a cheerful “Hello!” (heh-LOH).

name: Uruguay
arrival: This small country sits on South America's Atlantic coast between Brazil and Argentina. Known for wide grassy plains, cattle ranches, and sandy beaches, it is the birthplace of tango music and a towering steak sandwich called the chivito.

hints.text: studied a map of a small country squeezed between Brazil and Argentina on the Atlantic coast
joked about visiting a land with far more cattle than people, grazing on endless grassy plains
pinned on a flag badge: blue and white stripes with a golden smiling sun in the corner
asked the bank for a bundle of banknotes called the Uruguayan peso

greeting.text: People speak Spanish here, so say hello with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Venezuela
arrival: This country sits on the northern coast of South America. It is home to Angel Falls, the tallest waterfall on Earth, plus the grassy Llanos plains where capybaras, caimans, and anacondas live.

hints.text: planned a trip to the warm northern coast of South America, beside the Caribbean Sea
dreamed of standing under the tallest waterfall in the world, tumbling from a flat-topped mountain
wanted to spot capybaras, caimans, and giant anacondas out on wide grassy plains
traced a flag: yellow, blue, and red stripes topped with an arc of white stars
studied a guidebook page picturing colorful notes called the bolívar

greeting.text: People speak Spanish here, so greet someone with “Hola” (OH-lah).

name: Fiji
arrival: This nation of more than 330 islands in the South Pacific is famous for its warm turquoise sea, gardens of soft coral loved by divers, and the ceremonial sharing of a peppery drink called kava.

hints.text: booked a ticket toward a group of islands far out in the warm South Pacific
kept talking about a place where people walk barefoot across hot glowing stones
studied a flag in a guidebook: light blue, with a little Union Jack and a shield
swapped travelers' cheques for a roll of Fijian dollars

greeting.text: In Fijian, hello is “Bula” (BOO-lah) — it also means life and good health!

name: Kiribati
arrival: This country of low coral islands lies in the central Pacific, right where each new day on Earth begins — making it one of the first places to see the sunrise.

hints.text: couldn't wait to catch a sunrise where each brand-new day on Earth first begins
described tiny, flat islands so low that the sea is never more than a short walk away
packed a snorkel to swim over bright coral reefs full of fish
doodled a flag with a golden bird flying over a rising sun, above three white ocean waves

greeting.text: In the local language, Gilbertese, hello is “Mauri” (MAH-oo-ree).

name: Marshall Islands
arrival: This country is a scattered chain of low coral atolls in the central Pacific, barely rising above the waves. Long ago its sailors found their way using clever wooden "stick charts" that read the ocean's swells.

hints.text: wanted to dive down to sunken warships resting quietly on a lagoon floor
loved that this place made a giant safe zone where sharks are protected
sewed a flag patch on a backpack — dark blue, with orange-over-white stripes sweeping up to a white star

greeting.text: In Marshallese, hello is “Iọkwe” (YAWK-way) — it also wishes you love.

name: Micronesia
arrival: This country is spread across hundreds of islands in the western Pacific. It is famous for Nan Madol, an ancient stone city built on tiny man-made islands, and for the giant stone-disc money still prized on Yap.

hints.text: packed for island-hopping across a scattered country in the western Pacific
was amazed by an ancient stone city built on hundreds of little man-made islands
kept asking about an island where huge stone discs are used as money
drew a flag: plain light blue with four little white stars in a diamond

greeting.text: In Pohnpeian, hello is “Kaselehlie” (kah-seh-LEH-lee-eh).

name: Nauru
arrival: This tiny island in the central Pacific is one of the smallest countries on Earth — you can drive all the way around it in under half an hour. Years of digging up phosphate rock left its middle a rocky moonscape.

hints.text: wondered about a tiny speck of an island floating all alone in the central Pacific
was tickled that you could drive the whole way around it in under half an hour
was curious about an island whose middle was dug up into strange rocky pinnacles
wanted to visit one of the very smallest island countries in the whole world
doodled a blue flag with one thin yellow stripe across the middle and a single white star below it

greeting.text: In Nauruan, a warm welcome is “Ekamowir omo.”

name: New Zealand
arrival: These two large islands in the South Pacific are known for green mountains and misty fiords, bubbling geysers and mud pools, far more sheep than people, and the Māori haka — a powerful ceremonial dance.

hints.text: booked a ticket toward a pair of green islands way down in the South Pacific
kept giggling about a land that has far more sheep than people
stuck a flag sticker on a suitcase — blue with a Union Jack and four red stars of the Southern Cross
counted out crisp banknotes called the New Zealand dollar

greeting.text: In Māori, hello is “Kia ora” (KEE-ah OR-ah).

name: Samoa
arrival: This group of islands in the South Pacific sits at the heart of Polynesia. It is famous for hand-tapped tattoos, welcoming villages led by chiefs, and the deep, round To Sua swimming hole reached by a tall ladder.

hints.text: studied a map of a cluster of islands sitting at the very heart of Polynesia
planned to watch tattoos being tapped into skin by hand with tools used for hundreds of years
pinned on a flag badge: bright red with a small blue corner holding five white stars
packed a purse of leftover coins called the tala

greeting.text: In Samoan, hello is “Talofa” (tah-LOH-fah).

name: Solomon Islands
arrival: This chain of nearly a thousand tropical islands in the South Pacific is known for its warm lagoons, coral reefs, sunken World War II ships that divers love to explore, and a fiery underwater volcano nicknamed the Sharkcano.

hints.text: dreamed of peering at a hidden underwater volcano nicknamed the Sharkcano
packed scuba gear to dive over sunken warships from a big war long ago
sewed a flag patch on a backpack — blue and green split by a yellow diagonal stripe, five white stars in the corner
showed off a shiny coin called the Solomon Islands dollar

greeting.text: Many people speak Pijin — say hello with “Halo” (HAH-loh).

name: Tonga
arrival: This kingdom of scattered islands in the South Pacific is the only Pacific nation never colonized, and it still has its own king. It is known for friendly villages, ancient stone monuments, and warm seas where humpback whales come to visit.

hints.text: wanted to swim in warm blue water right beside giant humpback whales
kept talking about the last island nation still ruled by its very own king
traced a flag — mostly red with a white corner holding a red cross
asked the bank for a bundle of banknotes called the paʻanga

greeting.text: In Tongan, hello is “Mālō e lelei” (MAH-loh eh leh-LAY).

name: Vanuatu
arrival: This nation of about 80 islands in the South Pacific is known for its rumbling volcanoes, coral reefs, and the vine-jumping tradition that inspired bungee jumping.

hints.text: couldn't wait to climb a volcano and peer down into its glowing, bubbling top
kept talking about a place where people leap from tall wooden towers with vines tied to their feet — the very first bungee jump
showed off a flag pin — red and green with a black triangle and a little curled boar's tusk
changed a wad of cash into island money called the vatu

greeting.text: Most people speak Bislama, a playful cousin of English — say hello with “halo” (HAH-loh).
